title: The Damdami Taksal
hook: a school of recitation and exposition that traces itself to Baba Deep Singh

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nihang speech: sava lakh, one rider counted as an army. Your line was one is enough. Where did your bold name help? Day one thousand three hundred ten.

A coin from a careless mint looks almost right. The edge is a little soft, the face a little blurred, and after a while the shopkeepers start biting it to check. A coin from a careful mint is crisp. Every line is where it should be, and nobody has to bite it. Year one stood in the Japji's workshop, where the Word is struck in a true mint. Today we meet a school with the word mint in its own name, a school that sets out to strike readers of Gurbani as crisply as coins.
screen: `A CARELESS COIN GETS BITTEN.` → `A CAREFUL COIN IS CRISP.` → `A SCHOOL NAMED FOR A MINT.`

segments.voice: Taksal means a mint, the place where coins are struck. The Japji uses it in its thirty-eighth step, on Ang 8, in paraphrase: in the true mint, the Word is struck. The Damdami Taksal is a school of Sikh learning that carries that word in its name. Damdami points to Damdama Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo. Year three sat at the desk there with Baba Deep Singh, copying the Granth one letter at a time. The Taksal traces its line of teachers back to him, and through him, in its own telling, to Guru Gobind Singh at Damdama. So it is a chain: teacher to student, student to teacher, each one handing on the same careful way of reading. What does the school strike? Three things, mainly. First, recitation: reading Gurbani aloud, steadily and correctly. Second, exposition, which Sikhs call katha: explaining what the lines mean. Third, the way of life around both, kept in the school itself, where students live and learn together. The Taksal keeps its own rehat on some points, and Sikhs hold a range of views about where it and the wider panth's code agree and differ. Today stays with what it's known for: care. Here's why care with the sound matters to a school like this. Gurbani is meant to be heard and sung, not only read silently. A word slurred or misplaced can blur the meaning, the way a soft edge blurs a coin. So the students repeat, and repeat, and are corrected, until the line comes out crisp. Tomorrow we sit in on that teaching itself. For today, hold the picture: a mint for readers, and a chain of teachers reaching back to a desk at Damdama.
screen: `TAKSAL: A MINT.` · `A CHAIN BACK TO BABA DEEP SINGH.` · `RECITATION, KATHA, A WAY OF LIFE.` · `A SLURRED WORD BLURS THE MEANING.` · then, large: `CAREFUL READING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice one line's pronunciation. Settle, and breathe. Take the opening of the Mool Mantar, two words you've heard many times on this path: Ik Onkar. Say it silently, slowly, the way you'd hold a coin up to the light. Ik, on the in-breath. Onkar, on the out-breath. Don't hurry it. Let each sound land fully before the next. If your mind drifts, come back to the first sound. If you pray, you can let the line itself be the prayer. The bell holds the time.

Your line: careful reading. Today, read one paragraph aloud, slowly, as if every word had to come out crisp. Notice what you hear that you'd have missed. Day one thousand three hundred ten.
